enrichment.short_title: Immigration appeal on mental health and ECHR Articles 3 and 8
key_facts: David White, a Jamaican overstayer, appealed against removal after his grandmother's death and serious assaults in the UK left him with major depression and PTSD.
Dr Sen's unchallenged psychiatric evidence said return to Jamaica would substantially increase his risk of self-harm and suicidal behaviour.
The IAT held that removal would be a proportionate Article 8 interference and that Article 3 was not engaged; it granted limited leave to appeal on two grounds.
The Court of Appeal refused to hear a third ground for which leave had been refused and dismissed the appeal on Articles 3 and 8.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal on questions of law from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal after an adjudicator dismissed the appellant's human rights appeal against removal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; the court held the third ground could not be pursued without leave and that Articles 3 and 8 were not violated.
enrichment.ratio: On an appeal to the Court of Appeal under Schedule 4 paragraph 23 of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, an appellant may pursue only questions of law for which the IAT or the Court of Appeal has granted leave; where expert evidence of mental-health risk on removal is uncontradicted but treatment is available in the receiving state and the risk falls short of the high Article 3 threshold exemplified in Bensaid, removal may lawfully be a proportionate Article 8 interference.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant may pursue at the Court of Appeal a question of law on which the IAT refused leave
Whether the IAT irrationally treated Dr Sen's evidence on self-harm risk
Whether removal to Jamaica would breach ECHR Article 3
Whether removal would breach ECHR Article 8 family and private life rights

enrichment.short_title: Special Hours Certificate limited to basement with MDL
key_facts: Westminster appealed by case stated against justices who made final a Special Hours Certificate for both ground and basement floors of Elysium in the Café Royal complex.
A Music and Dancing Licence covered only the basement, while the SHC as granted extended to both floors until 3am.
Westminster argued section 77A required an MDL for the same physical area as any SHC and feared a late-night ground-floor bar.
The licensees accepted for the appeal that the MDL restriction to the basement was effective.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated to the High Court (Administrative Court) from Horseferry Road licensing justices.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the SHC was declared to apply to the basement floor only; permission to appeal and a stay were granted.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 77A of the Licensing Act 1964, licensing justices may grant a special hours certificate only for premises or a part of premises for which a music and dancing licence is in force; where an MDL covers only the basement, a provisional or final SHC for the whole of Elysium was beyond power even though music and dancing were provided elsewhere on the licensed premises.
legal_issues: Whether section 77A(1)(a)(ii) permits an SHC for licensed premises wider than the area covered by the MDL
Whether the concluding words of section 77A(1) allow an SHC for a larger area than the MDL
Whether section 81(2) adequately protects against misuse of an over-wide SHC

enrichment.short_title: Drug conviction appeal over late-disclosed pocket note
key_facts: Shahhed Boksh was convicted of possessing class A drugs with intent to supply after a search of 24 Bramble House in February 2001.
During trial a paper with drug-dealing notations was found inside the security bag with £215 cash taken from his pocket, though it was not recorded in the Premises Search Book.
The judge refused to adjourn, discharge the jury, or exclude the evidence; the jury were told there was no evidence of who wrote on the paper.
The Court of Appeal held the disclosure failure was not deliberate misconduct and the conviction was safe on the overall evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the conviction was held safe despite imperfect summing-up on the pocket paper.
enrichment.ratio: Where police inadvertently fail to record a small paper found with seized cash and disclose it promptly once discovered, that does not amount to the serious abuse of process required to stay proceedings or discharge the jury; section 78 exclusion and an adjournment for forensic testing were rightly refused where the Crown relied on the document only for its similarity to other dealing records and abundant other evidence supported guilt.
legal_issues: Whether non-disclosure of the pocket paper before trial was an abuse of process
Whether the judge should have adjourned or discharged the jury for handwriting or DNA testing
Whether admission of the paper under section 78 was unfair
Whether the jury direction on authorship of the writing was adequate

R v Keane
R v Winston Brown

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of section 101A public sewer duty
key_facts: Welsh Water sought judicial review of two Environment Agency Wales decisions imposing a section 101A duty to provide public sewers at Llantilio Pertholey and Rhoseberse Road.
Pollution from some septic tanks was accepted, but Welsh Water proposed cesspools as a cheaper private alternative to mains sewerage.
The Agency extended the duty to additional premises likely to suffer adverse effects and rejected cesspools by policy preference.
Welsh Water adduced fresh post-decision engineering evidence which the court considered de bene esse but largely excluded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of two linked Environment Agency determinations under section 101A(7) of the Water Industry Act 1991.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; both Agency decisions were held lawful on the evidence before the decision-maker.
enrichment.ratio: Where a sewerage undertaker has been put on notice that the Environment Agency is considering additional premises in a locality and supplies geological and technical information on which the Agency reasonably finds likely adverse environmental effects, the Agency may lawfully impose a section 101A public sewer duty beyond the originally polluting properties; a general preference for public sewers over cesspools is lawful if applied flexibly to the individual case, and fresh evidence on judicial review is admissible only within narrow Powis categories.
legal_issues: Whether the Agency erred in extending the sewerage duty to premises without direct evidence of pollution
Whether the Agency failed the section 101A(2) and (3) balancing exercise
Whether the Agency inflexibly applied an anti-cesspool policy
Whether cost comparisons between public and private sewerage options were material errors
Admissibility of fresh engineering evidence on judicial review

enrichment.short_title: Marshland flooding, nuisance duty and drainage easement
key_facts: John Green owns Priory Marshes in Norfolk and claimed flooding from Fritton Lake and neighbouring Scale Marshes owned by Somerleyton estate trustees.
Heavy rainfall in December 1993 flooded Priory Marshes after the shared drainage pump failed when blocked by eels; the Blocka Run had silted up.
The judge dismissed Rylands v Fletcher and nuisance claims and declared the trustees had an implied easement to drain lake water through dykes on Priory Marshes.
The Court of Appeal held a Leakey duty could arise for naturally flowing floodwater but the trustees had not breached it and the easement claim succeeded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from a Chancery Division trial on nuisance and counterclaim for a drainage easement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; cross-appeal allowed on prescriptive easement; declaration of drainage easement upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Thomas does not exclude a Leakey duty in respect of naturally flowing floodwater, but where marshes are natural receptors for upper-catchment water, longstanding 1958 drainage arrangements allocate responsibility reasonably and neighbours must identify remedial steps sought; the 1921 conveyance and drainage deed impliedly reserved to Scale Marshes an easement to drain naturally arriving water, including from Fritton Lake, through existing dykes on Priory Marshes.
legal_issues: Whether Thomas excludes a Leakey duty for naturally flowing water
Whether trustees breached a duty of care by failing to maintain the Blocka Run
Whether the 1921 conveyance impliedly reserved an easement including lake water
Whether a prescriptive drainage easement arose by lost modern grant

enrichment.short_title: Czech extradition habeas corpus triviality challenge
key_facts: Milan Scuka challenged detention under two Bow Street committal orders following Czech extradition requests for prison bullying and a purse theft worth about £2.80.
He argued both offences were trivial under section 11(3)(a) and that extradition should await his pending asylum appeal.
The harassment warrant alleged forcing a younger inmate to perform chores and isolating him in a shared cell.
The court held neither offence was trivial and that extradition need not be adjourned for the asylum process.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Divisional Court applications for habeas corpus challenging committal orders in extradition proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications refused; bail reporting varied and leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 11(3)(a) of the Extradition Act 1989 requires a case-by-case assessment of triviality by the nature and quality of the conduct, not the monetary value alone; bullying of a vulnerable younger prisoner and theft from an elderly victim are not trivial, and extradition proceedings should generally continue pending asylum determination following Karpichov & Marais.
legal_issues: Whether the Czech offences were trivial under section 11(3)(a)
Whether a proportionality test applies to the triviality threshold
Whether the bullying charge corresponded to an English harassment offence
Whether extradition should be stayed pending asylum appeal

enrichment.short_title: Pub assault damages for frontal lobe brain injury
key_facts: Craig Marchent, aged 23, was assaulted by pub doormen in Bristol in July 1996, sustaining head, wrist and knee injuries after a 60% liability judgment against Allied Domecq.
He had a long history of violence, dyslexia, low IQ and antisocial behaviour, but witnesses said his conduct improved before the assault.
Joint experts agreed orthopaedic injuries limited heavy work; disputed psychiatrists disagreed on permanent frontal lobe damage and capacity.
The judge found frontal lobe injury had permanently worsened behaviour and declared him a patient unable to manage his affairs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court assessment of damages after interlocutory judgment on liability; Official Solicitor acted as litigation friend.
enrichment.outcome: Damages assessed including general damages, loss of earnings, care, case management and Court of Protection costs; structured settlement to be considered.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant with pre-existing antisocial personality disorder and marginal capacity sustains a significant occipital blow causing permanent frontal lobe deficits evidenced by neuropsychological testing, tortfeasors remain liable for attributable behavioural deterioration and care needs; capacity to manage affairs depends on executive function and insight under the Mental Health Act 1983 and Masterman-Lister principles, not IQ alone.
legal_issues: Whether the assault caused significant long-term brain injury or only exacerbated pre-existing disorder
Whether the claimant was a patient under the Mental Health Act 1983
Extent of loss of earning capacity and future care needs
Quantum of orthopaedic and psychiatric damages

enrichment.short_title: Part III financial claim 33 years after divorce

statutes_considered.title: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1976

key_facts: Cesa M and Richard L divorced in South Africa in 1973 after a short marriage and separated in 1970; she had relied on informal child support and rent-free occupation of a London flat.
Standing orders of £300 per month stopped in 2001 after a banking error, prompting a Part III claim for housing and income worth nearly £1 million.
The husband, domiciled in South Africa, had substantial trust wealth; the wife had limited capital spent on litigation costs.
The court held the 1973 arrangement was not a binding clean break but awarded modest maintenance and 50% of net sale proceeds if she left the flat.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application for financial relief after overseas divorce under Part III of the Matrimonial and Family Proceedings Act 1984 following grant of leave.
enrichment.outcome: Part III threshold satisfied; lump sum £30,000 for repairs, £150,000 capitalised maintenance, £1,000 per month pension, and 50% of net proceeds on sale of the flat; clean break ordered.
enrichment.ratio: A Part III claim may proceed decades after an overseas divorce where the applicant remained financially dependent on informal support and no effective Edgar clean break existed; fairness may require limited maintenance reflecting carer contribution and need, but an outright transfer of a high-value home after a short marriage is disproportionate where statutory tenancy security already exists.
legal_issues: Whether it was appropriate to entertain a Part III application after 33 years
Whether the 1973 South African order amounted to a final clean break
Application of section 25 Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 factors
Appropriate housing and income provision for a dependent former spouse
linked_authorities: Edgar v Edgar

confidence.notes: Full first-instance judgment with section 16 threshold and section 25 analysis clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: VAT on motor breakdown insurance claims handling

statutes_considered.title: Value Added Tax (Input Tax) (Specified Supplies) Order 1999

key_facts: WHA Ltd handled motor breakdown insurance claims for Gibraltar-based Viscount Re under a Project C restructuring of NIG policies sold through car dealers.
Approved garages repaired insured vehicles and invoiced WHA, which paid from a claims float funded by Viscount.
The VAT Tribunal held garages supplied the insured, not WHA, and that only part of WHA's service to Viscount was exempt claims handling.
The High Court held garages made a taxable supply to WHA used in its business and that WHA's entire service to Viscount was a single exempt insurance-related supply.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from VAT and Duties Tribunal decisions on linked input tax and exemption issues.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the first two issues in WHA's favour; third issue not decided; respondent's notice arguments reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Where a garage repairs an insured's car under WHA's authority and invoices WHA, the garage supplies services to WHA for consideration which WHA uses to perform its claims-handling obligations, giving WHA input tax; WHA's procurement and payment of authorised repairs form one indivisible exempt insurance intermediary service under Schedule 9 Group 2 rather than a separate taxable satisfaction of claims.
legal_issues: Whether garages make a taxable supply of repair services to WHA or only to the insured
Whether WHA's supply to Viscount is wholly exempt insurance-related services
Whether Note (10) excludes payment of garage invoices from exemption
Whether Viscount could recover input tax if WHA charged VAT

enrichment.short_title: Change-of-control clause in EBUK services agreement
key_facts: EBUK sought to terminate a 1995 services agreement with EBI using a change-of-control clause after Kim family interests in the service provider fell below 50%.
The agreement allowed EBUK to terminate if control passed from persons exercising it at the date of the contract, with control defined by share ownership or policy direction.
EBI reorganised into a Pennsylvania limited liability partnership novated to EBS, where Mr Kim retained direction through the general partner despite reduced equity.
The judge held control remained with the same persons through the right to direct policies and affairs even after the shareholding change.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from a High Court decision on construction of a termination clause in a services agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; EBUK had no right to terminate for change of control.
enrichment.ratio: A reciprocal change-of-control clause requiring control to pass from the persons exercising it at the contract date must first identify who exercised control under the composite definition; where the Kim family both owned more than 50% and directed affairs through the general partner at novation, later reduction of beneficial ownership below 50% without loss of directional control does not trigger termination.
legal_issues: Construction of 'control' in clause 14.1(d) and analogous clause 14.2(b)
Whether ownership below 50% alone triggers termination despite retained directional control
Application of the reciprocal change-of-control provision to EBUK and EBI/EBS
linked_authorities: Reardon Smith Line Ltd v Yngvar Hansen-Tangen

confidence.notes: Focused construction appeal with agreed corporate structure charts and clear ratio on control definition.
